The origins of the Dutch water boards, or *waterschappen*, lie in the unique geographical challenge of the Low Countries. Much of the land was either below sea level or constantly threatened by rivers and the sea. ### The Venetian Republic: A History of the Serenissima

The Most Serene Republic of Venice, known as *La Serenissima*, was a maritime and commercial power that endured for over a millennium. Rising from a collection of refugee settlements in a malarial lagoon, it grew into a formidable empire that dominated the Mediterranean, acting as a crucial bridge between East and West. Its unique political system, blending oligarchy and republicanism, and its singular focus on commerce and stability, allowed it to survive the fall of empires and shape the course of European history.

# A History of Printing, by Era

## The Ancient World: Seals, Stamps, and the First Impressions

Long before anyone conceived of a printing press, humans were pressing inked surfaces onto other surfaces. The earliest ancestors of printing are the cylinder seals of Mesopotamia, carved stone rollers that were pressed into wet clay to leave repeating images and cuneiform inscriptions, used from around 3500 BCE to authenticate documents and mark goods. Ancient Egypt contributed the practice of stamping, and by the time of the Roman Empire, terracotta and metal stamps were in common use for marking bricks, amphorae, and loaves of bread. The Romans also developed the *signaculum*, a stamp used to seal documents, and the practice of taking impressions from engraved gems. # A History of Public Libraries

## Antiquity and the Ancient World: Precursors of the Public Library

Long before the invention of the codex or the printing press, the impulse to gather and preserve written knowledge for communal use took root in the ancient world. In Mesopotamia, the library of Ashurbanipal at Nineveh, assembled in the seventh century BCE, collected thousands of clay tablets on subjects ranging from astronomy to law, and although it served a royal court rather than a general public, it established the idea that a collection of records could be organized, cataloged, and made available to readers beyond a single scribe. In Egypt, the legendary Library of Alexandria, founded in the third century BCE under the Ptolemaic dynasty, aspired to gather copies of every book in the known world; it functioned as a research institution and, in a limited sense, as a semi-public scholarly resource, attracting intellectuals from across the Mediterranean.
